title: How to Eat and Feast Without Guilt or Excess
excerpt: Almost none of us simply eat. We manage, we reward, we punish, we apologize. The table was meant to be a place of gratitude and communion before it was ever a matter of nutrition.
body:
Watch how people eat and you will see what they believe about themselves. For some, food is comfort, the thing the hand reaches for when the day has emptied them out. For some it is control, the one corner of a chaotic life that will still obey. For some it is guilt, every meal arriving with a verdict attached, a running tally of what has been earned and what must now be repaid. Almost none of us simply eat. We manage, we reward, we punish, we apologize. The plain act of receiving food with thanks has become rare.

The two failures here mirror each other. There is excess, the appetite that has become its own master, that eats past fullness and past gratitude into numbness. And there is its respectable twin, the obsessive control that treats every bite as a moral event, that has turned the table into a courtroom. The church has tended to thunder against the first and quietly admire the second, calling it discipline. Scripture is suspicious of both.

## A word that has to come first

Before anything else. If eating has become frightening, or compulsive, or tangled up with punishment, if you skip meals out of fear or eat in secret out of shame or cannot sit at a table without a war going on inside you, that is not a willpower problem and not a faith problem to be prayed away alone. It is a medical and psychological matter, and a serious one. See a doctor. See a counselor. God is not ashamed of you for needing help, and getting it is an act of faith, not a failure of it. Nothing else in this piece applies until that is said.

## The table before the label

The modern food environment is engineered to make us eat badly and constantly. We are being discipled by packaging and marketing far more than by any wisdom, taught to think of eating as fuel and nutrients and macros, a delivery system for the body rather than a human practice. Recovering the meal as a meal is most of the battle.

Scripture treats food as gift before it is ever nutrition. Everything God created is good, Paul writes to Timothy, and is to be received with thanksgiving. That single word reframes the whole thing. Eating is meant to be an act of gratitude and communion, a daily return to the God who made wheat and fish and oil and the tongue that tastes them. The center of eating is not the label. It is the table, and the thanks said over it.

## Jesus came eating

It is worth saying loudly, especially to the guilt-bound, that Jesus came eating and drinking, and his enemies called him a glutton and a drunkard for it. He was forever at someone's table. He made wine at a wedding when the wine ran out. His first miracle was not feeding a fast. It was keeping a feast going. The kingdom of God, in his own image for it, is a banquet.

So a Christianity of perpetual anxious restriction slanders the Giver. If every meal is a guilty negotiation, something has gone wrong with your theology before anything has gone wrong with your diet. Food is a gift, and the right response to a gift is thanks, not apology. You are allowed to enjoy your dinner. You are allowed to feast.

## And freedom that can still say no

But hear the other side, because grace is not the same as appetite. The same Paul who calls all food good also says he will not be mastered by anything. Freedom that never declines anything has quietly become appetite with a verse attached. The feast is good precisely because it is a feast and not the daily condition, an arrival that means something because there are ordinary days around it.

The practice, then, is not a rule about quantities. It is the slow recovery of eating as gift, which heals both ditches at once. The glutton learns that more is not the way to satisfaction, because the joy was never in the volume. The anxious controller learns that food is allowed, that thanks can replace the audit. Both are being led to the same plain table, where you receive what is given, eat it with gratitude, and stop without ceremony when you have had enough.

## Feasting is a discipline too

We think of discipline as restraint, but feasting takes its own discipline, the discipline of actually being present and grateful instead of distracted and numb. Eating one meal slowly, with thanks, no screen in sight, tasting the food and noticing that it was given, is harder than skipping a meal for many of us. It requires you to be in your body, at a table, receiving. That is a spiritual act, and most of us have lost the muscle for it.

## This week

Eat one meal slowly this week, with thanks, with no screen anywhere in sight. Taste the food. Name one specific thing on the table you are grateful for, out loud, the bread, the person across from you, the fact that there is enough. And once this week, if your history allows it, let yourself genuinely feast, a real meal with people, enjoyed without the running tally, received as the gift it is. You are not on a program. You are learning, slowly, to do the oldest and simplest thing, to receive your food from God's hand and say thank you.
